claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength because its uniform single-phase solid solution provides low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction in CoCrFeNiTi promotes easy dislocation glide.
CoCrFeNiTi does not substantially engage work-hardening mechanisms such as deformation twinning or transformation-induced phase changes under the specified conditions.
The applicable initial material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a homogeneous single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
Mechanical deformation combined with TEM or EBSD can be used to characterize the operative deformation mechanisms.
The proposed loading regime is room-temperature quasi-static deformation at a strain rate of approximately 10^-3 s^-1.
Dislocation mobility and dislocation density in the single-phase matrix are the structural mediators of the mechanical response.
The deformed CoCrFeNiTi microstructure will lack substantial deformation-induced twins or hcp regions that would impede dislocation flow.
The chemically complex but compositionally balanced CoCrFeNiTi lattice has only moderate local distortions, which are insufficient to act as strong dislocation obstacles.
Dislocations in single-phase CoCrFeNiTi glide without substantial accumulation at pinning points.
The absence of fcc-to-hcp transformation or nanotwinning suppresses work hardening and thereby lowers hardness and strength.
Deformation-induced nanotwins have been observed in related CrCoNi or CrMnFeCoNi alloys after extensive deformation.
CoCrFeNiTi will have lower yield strength and hardness than CoCrFeNi without Ti or alloys that activate transformation or twinning mechanisms.
The deformation microstructure of CoCrFeNiTi will be dominated by relatively mobile dislocations and show minimal twins or phase transformations.
Easy dislocation glide accounts for the reported favorable plasticity associated with the low hardness and strength.
The hypothesis applies only to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state under room-temperature quasi-static loading.
Additional nanoscale phases or major processing-induced microstructural changes may invalidate the proposed easy-glide mechanism.
Ti may promote short-range chemical ordering or minor segregation under some processing conditions, thereby changing dislocation behavior.
Small changes in chemical order may alter stacking-fault energy enough to favor other deformation modes.
Observation of pronounced nanotwinning or a detectable fcc-to-hcp transformation that contributes to work hardening would falsify the hypothesis.
